text_key: ## One-Sentence Summary This initiative proposes a federal policy and incentive program to accelerate the reduction of air pollutant emissions from ports and ships by mandating and subsidizing a transition to on-shore power for vessels at berth, requiring the use of ultra-low-sulphur marine fuels within UAE territorial waters, and modernizing all registered harbor-craft to run on electricity or approved clean fuels within a defined timeline. ## Problem While dust is a major contributor to PM levels, human-made pollution, including emissions from ports and shipping, significantly impacts air quality. Ships at berth typically burn marine diesel in auxiliary engines, emitting NO2, SO2, and PM, which contribute to ground-level ozone formation and particulate matter concentrations in coastal cities. Harbor-craft (tugs, barges, supply vessels) often use older, high-emission engines. Although UAE diesel fuel standards are stringent, marine fuel standards within territorial waters are not explicitly defined, and the use of shore power to eliminate at-berth emissions is not widespread. These emissions degrade local air quality, posing health risks to port-adjacent communities and workers, and conflict with the goals of the National Air Quality Agenda 2031 and the Net Zero by 2050 initiative. ## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases Primary beneficiaries would be communities living and working near major ports like Jebel Ali, Khalifa Port, Port Rashid, and Fujairah Port, who would experience reduced exposure to ship-based pollutants. The shipping industry, including vessel operators and port authorities, would benefit from structured regulatory clarity and financial support for transition. The initiative would also target owners and operators of the UAE's fleet of harbor-craft, which are critical for port operations but are emission-intensive. ## Solution / Service Overview The proposed NGPSI would have three core components: (1) A federal regulation requiring all major commercial ports to provide and mandate the use of shore power (cold ironing) for compatible vessels at berth by a proposed target date. (2) A federal regulation establishing an Emission Control Area (ECA) within UAE territorial waters, mandating the use of marine fuels with a sulphur content not exceeding 0.1% for all ships. (3) A federal grant and low-interest loan program to support the retrofitting or replacement of registered harbor-craft with electric or clean-fuel (e.g., hydrogen, LNG) propulsion systems. ## Delivery Model The initiative could be overseen by a proposed inter-agency task force led by MOCCAE, in collaboration with the Federal Transport Authority – Land & Maritime, port authorities (e.g., DP World, AD Ports Group), and the Emirates Maritime Arbitration Centre. Regulatory development and phased implementation would be centralized at the federal level to ensure consistency. Financial incentives would be administered through a proposed dedicated fund. Port authorities would be responsible for the infrastructure rollout, with technical standards set by the federal regulator. ## Funding & Sustainability Initial funding could be sought from a combination of federal budget allocation aligned with the National Air Quality Agenda and a proposed modest, per-tonne levy on cargo handled at participating ports, creating a dedicated "Green Ports Fund." This fund would finance port electrification infrastructure and provide matching grants for harbor-craft modernization. Long-term sustainability would derive from reduced public health costs, alignment with the UAE's net-zero goals, and potential for ports to attract "green" shipping customers, creating a competitive advantage. ## What Makes It New While individual emirates or ports may have environmental programs, this proposal creates a unified, nationwide regulatory framework specifically targeting the maritime sector's air pollution levers. It combines a mandatory territorial ECA (which would be a first for the region) with a comprehensive shore power mandate and a targeted modernization program for the localized harbor-craft fleet, addressing both ocean-going and domestic maritime sources in one integrated policy. ## Measuring Impact Success would be measured by tracking proposed indicators: (1) Percentage of vessel calls at major ports using shore power. (2) Reduction in average SO2 and NO2 concentrations measured at monitoring stations within 5km of major ports. (3) Number of harbor-craft retrofitted or replaced under the grant program. (4) Estimated annual reductions in tonnes of SO2, NOx, and PM2.5 emissions from the maritime sector, as calculated using a proposed updated federal emissions inventory methodology. ## Risks & Mitigation Key risks include: (1) High upfront capital costs for port infrastructure and vessel retrofits, mitigated by phased implementation and the proposed financial incentive program. (2) Technical compatibility challenges with diverse vessel types, mitigated by developing a proposed standardized technical framework and prioritizing high-traffic vessel categories. (3) Potential for increased operational costs for shipping lines, mitigated by clear long-term regulatory certainty and the proposed ECA potentially driving regional adoption, leveling the playing field. (4) Regulatory coordination between federal and local port authorities, mitigated by the proposed inter-agency task force structure designed to ensure alignment.

text_key: ## One-Sentence Summary A proposed UAE airport ground-operations programme would pilot electric ground-support equipment, cleaner fuel controls, dust suppression, and micro air-quality monitoring to reduce local PM2.5, NO2, and ozone precursor exposure. ## Problem UAE air quality remains far above WHO guidelines: IQAir gave UAE PM2.5 as 36.4 µg/m³ in 2025, 7.3 times the WHO annual guideline, and EAD named particulate matter and ground-level ozone as Abu Dhabi's pollutants of major concern. Summer ozone peaks in July and August and correlates strongly with temperature, while the NO2 annual guideline is 10 µg/m³. The National Air Quality Agenda 2031 reportedly targets 90% compliance with a national PM2.5 standard by 2040. Aviation ground operations, if included in source controls, could create local hotspots through diesel equipment, idling, apron dust, and fuel handling. The initiative addresses this potential source without relying only on long-range transport or natural dust, which an Abu Dhabi study found contributed about 40% and 25% of PM2.5 in 2012. ## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases Primary beneficiaries would be airport workers, passengers, and nearby residents exposed to ground-level pollutants. Proposed use cases include replacing diesel baggage tractors, catering vehicles, pushback equipment, and apron buses with electric or lower-emission alternatives; testing cleaner diesel and fuel-system controls; managing dust on aprons and service roads; and installing micro-stations to map PM2.5, PM10, NO2, and ozone around aircraft movement areas. ## Solution / Service Overview The initiative would create a proposed Airport Clean Ground Operations Pilot at selected aviation sites. It would combine three services: a ground-support-equipment electrification and maintenance standard, aligned with the National EV Policy target of EVs making up 50% of vehicles by 2050; a fuel and emissions control service requiring UAE diesel to meet the 10 ppm sulphur and Euro 5 standard, with proposed spot checks informed by the fact that 62% of inspected Dubai companies were using off-specification diesel in 2019; and an air-quality micro-monitoring and dust-management service that would publish proposed dashboards for operators. The pilot would test whether electrification, cleaner fuels, and dust controls can reduce local PM2.5 and NO2 while supporting the Net Zero by 2050 initiative. ## Delivery Model Delivery would be phased. First, a proposed baseline would map pollutant concentrations and equipment fleets at pilot sites, using data formats compatible with MOCCAE reclassified monitoring stations and EAD/Dubai Municipality networks. Second, a proposed procurement and operations plan would phase electric equipment into baggage, catering, and apron services. Third, a proposed compliance and training programme would cover fuel checks, dust suppression, and maintenance. Governance could be handled by a proposed airport-level task force with operators, fuel suppliers, equipment vendors, and air-quality authorities. ## Funding & Sustainability Funding could combine proposed airport capital budgets, vendor financing, and green-finance instruments, without assuming existing budgets. Sustainability would depend on lower fuel and maintenance costs, alignment with the Net Zero by 2050 initiative, and possible savings from meeting WHO guidelines, estimated by an Economist Impact 2025 analysis at US$596 million a year nationally. A proposed fee or rebate mechanism could support equipment replacement for smaller operators. ## What Makes It New Most existing UAE air-quality focus areas in the brief name oil and gas, road transport, and industry. This proposal shifts attention to aviation ground operations as a local, controllable source, pairing equipment electrification with micro-scale monitoring and dust management rather than relying only on ambient-station averages. ## Measuring Impact Proposed indicators: share of electric or low-emission ground-support equipment; fuel sulphur compliance checks; PM2.5, PM10, NO2, and ozone readings at apron micro-stations; dust-control incidents; and worker exposure estimates. Success would be tested against WHO annual guidelines (PM2.5 5 µg/m³, PM10 15 µg/m³, NO2 10 µg/m³) and national AQI limits. ## Risks & Mitigation Risks include high upfront equipment costs, limited electric GSE availability, dust-storm interference with monitoring, and data gaps. Mitigations: phased replacement, maintenance contracts, mobile monitoring during dust episodes, and transparent reporting. Because about 90% of UAE dust episodes come from the southwest and dust storms peak in winter, the pilot would separate dust signals from combustion signals using PM2.5/PM10 ratios and NO2 trends.

text_key: ## One-Sentence Summary This initiative proposes a federal regulation and incentive program to mandate the capture and productive use of associated petroleum gas (APG) currently flared, vented, or leaked from oil and gas operations, converting a major source of air pollutants into a commercial asset. ## Problem Flaring, venting, and fugitive methane leaks from oil and gas operations are a significant source of air pollutants, including nitrogen oxides (NOx), sulfur dioxide (SO2), volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and particulate matter (PM). Captured gas could be used for on-site power generation, injected into the national gas grid, used as feedstock for petrochemicals, or converted into hydrogen or compressed natural gas for transportation. ## Solution / Service Overview The proposed solution is a two-part federal framework: (1) A **Regulatory Mandate** setting progressively stricter limits on flaring and venting, with a goal of near-zero routine flaring by 2035, enforced through continuous monitoring and reporting. (2) A **Monetization Support Program** to facilitate compliance by providing technical assistance, sharing best practices for leak detection and repair (LDAR), and co-investing in shared gas-gathering infrastructure in fields where individual operator investment is prohibitive. The program would prioritize capturing gas from the largest and most polluting sites first. ## Delivery Model The initiative would be delivered through a proposed public-private task force, potentially overseen by the Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure in coordination with the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment (MOCCAE). The regulatory component would involve setting and enforcing standards. The support program would operate as a dedicated unit offering feasibility studies, technology catalogs, and facilitating partnerships between operators and off-takers (e.g., power utilities, industrial users). ## Funding & Sustainability Initial funding for the support program's administrative and co-investment functions could be proposed from a dedicated portion of existing environmental fees or a proposed levy on continued flaring above benchmarked levels. It proposes a systematic, infrastructure-based approach rather than relying solely on penalties. ## Measuring Impact Success would be measured by: (1) **Direct Emission Reductions**: Quantified decreases in tonnes of NOx, SO2, VOCs, and methane reported by operators. (2) **Flaring Volumes**: Annual reduction in volumes of gas flared, targeting a proposed 95% reduction in routine flaring by 2035. (3) **Economic Output**: Cubic meters of gas captured and monetized annually. It moves beyond monitoring and general warnings to actively treating identified source zones. The proposed use of advanced soil stabilisation techniques combined with native-species greening tailored to the arid UAE environment represents a focused, nature-based engineering approach not yet deployed at a national scale for this purpose. ## Measuring Impact Success would be measured by proposed key performance indicators: 1) Reduction in PM10 concentrations during forecasted dust events in target downwind urban areas. 2) Increase in the accuracy and lead time of dust event warnings. 3) Hectares of dust-source hotspots stabilised and greened annually. 4) Tracking public and institutional adoption of the early warning system. 5) Monitoring trends in the PM2.5/PM10 ratio to isolate the impact on dust-driven pollution. ## Risks & Mitigation Key risks include: 1) **Technological failure of forecasts**: Mitigated by using ensemble models and continuous validation against monitoring station data. 2) **High cost and water needs for greening**: Mitigated by using drip irrigation with treated wastewater and selecting ultra-drought-tolerant native species. 3) **Slow visible results**: Mitigated by launching with a high-profile pilot zone to demonstrate efficacy and build support. 4) **Cross-emirate coordination challenges**: Mitigated by establishing clear federal leadership and aligning with existing national agendas.

## One-Sentence Summary
A proposed federal initiative to deploy advanced dust forecasting, targeted land stabilisation, and strategic greening to directly reduce the population's exposure to particulate matter from natural dust and sandstorms.

## Problem
Elevated levels of particulate matter (PM), particularly PM10 and PM2.5, are a persistent air quality challenge in the UAE, with studies in Abu Dhabi indicating a PM2.5/PM10 ratio generally below 0.5, pointing to dust as a primary driver. While human-made sources are significant, natural mineral dust contributed about 25% of PM2.5 in Abu Dhabi in 2012, and dust events most frequently originate from the southwest and peak in spring. This natural dust exacerbates pollution levels, contributing to health impacts and hindering progress toward national air quality targets and WHO guidelines.

## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases
The primary beneficiaries are the general public, whose health is impacted by poor air quality, and high-risk groups such as children, the elderly, and those with respiratory conditions. Key use cases include providing advanced warning to schools, construction sites, ports, and healthcare facilities to modify outdoor activities; guiding municipal operations like street cleaning; and protecting critical infrastructure from high-dust events.

## Solution / Service Overview
The proposed initiative would establish an integrated system with three core components: 1) A high-resolution, AI-enhanced dust forecasting and early warning platform capable of predicting the intensity and trajectory of dust events 48-72 hours in advance. 2) A targeted land stabilisation program focusing on identified dust-source hotspots, especially in the southwestern region, using sustainable soil binders and windbreak fencing. 3) A strategic ‘greening for dust suppression’ program that deploys drought-resistant, native ground-cover vegetation in stabilised areas and along key transport corridors to anchor soil.

## Delivery Model
Delivery would be coordinated by a proposed cross-emirate task force under federal leadership, leveraging existing monitoring networks. The forecasting platform would be developed in a proposed partnership with national and international meteorological research institutes. Land stabilisation and greening would be implemented through contracted specialists, with oversight from environmental agencies. Warnings and air quality information would be disseminated via a dedicated public app and integrated into existing government alert systems.

## Funding & Sustainability
Initial funding could be sought from federal budgets aligned with the National Air Quality Agenda 2031 and the Net Zero by 2050 strategic initiative. A proposed long-term sustainability model could explore public-private partnerships, where businesses benefiting from reduced operational disruptions (e.g., aviation, construction) contribute to a maintenance fund. Grants from global environmental and climate funds could also be pursued for the greening components.

## What Makes It New
While dust forecasting exists, this initiative proposes a novel integration of hyper-local forecasting with targeted, data-driven physical intervention on the ground. It moves beyond monitoring and general warnings to actively treating identified source zones. The proposed use of advanced soil stabilisation techniques combined with native-species greening tailored to the arid UAE environment represents a focused, nature-based engineering approach not yet deployed at a national scale for this purpose.

## Measuring Impact
Success would be measured by proposed key performance indicators: 1) Reduction in PM10 concentrations during forecasted dust events in target downwind urban areas. 2) Increase in the accuracy and lead time of dust event warnings. 3) Hectares of dust-source hotspots stabilised and greened annually. 4) Tracking public and institutional adoption of the early warning system. 5) Monitoring trends in the PM2.5/PM10 ratio to isolate the impact on dust-driven pollution.

## Risks & Mitigation
Key risks include: 1) **Technological failure of forecasts**: Mitigated by using ensemble models and continuous validation against monitoring station data. 2) **High cost and water needs for greening**: Mitigated by using drip irrigation with treated wastewater and selecting ultra-drought-tolerant native species. 3) **Slow visible results**: Mitigated by launching with a high-profile pilot zone to demonstrate efficacy and build support. 4) **Cross-emirate coordination challenges**: Mitigated by establishing clear federal leadership and aligning with existing national agendas.

text_key: ## One-Sentence Summary This initiative proposes the development of a federal Indoor Air Quality (IAQ) Enhancement Framework, featuring a government-backed certification and incentive program for the widespread deployment of high-efficiency filtration in air-conditioning (AC) systems and standalone air cleaners within homes, schools, and offices. ## Problem While outdoor air quality initiatives exist, individuals spend the majority of their time indoors, where air pollution can also concentrate. Data indicates that PM2.5 and PM10 levels in the UAE significantly exceed WHO annual guidelines, with dust being a primary driver. Although AC systems are ubiquitous, their standard filters are typically ineffective at capturing fine particulate matter (PM2.5), leaving indoor environments vulnerable to infiltration of outdoor pollutants. This creates a critical health exposure gap, especially for vulnerable groups, undermining public health gains from outdoor emission reductions. ## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases Primary beneficiaries include residents in high-exposure areas, children in public and private schools, and employees in both government and private-sector offices. A proposed initial focus could be on vulnerable populations, including the elderly and those with respiratory conditions, as well as educational facilities where children's developing lungs are particularly susceptible. Use cases center on retrofitting existing AC systems with high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) or MERV-13+ filters and deploying standalone air purifiers in spaces where central system upgrades are impractical. ## Solution / Service Overview The proposed solution is a three-pillar framework: 1) A Federal IAQ Standard for Public Buildings, mandating minimum filtration efficiency (e.g., MERV-13) for new and retrofitted AC systems in schools, government offices, and healthcare facilities; 2) An IAQ Certification & Incentive Program for private residences and commercial buildings, offering subsidies, low-interest loans, or utility rebates for the installation of certified high-performance filtration systems; and 3) A Public Awareness Campaign on IAQ management, including guidance on filter maintenance and the benefits of air purification. ## Delivery Model The initiative would require collaboration between federal and emirate-level entities. A proposed governance structure could involve MOCCAE setting the federal standards and framework, while local municipalities (e.g., Dubai Municipality, Abu Dhabi's EAD) oversee implementation and enforcement within their jurisdictions. Partnerships with AC manufacturers, filter producers, and certified installers would be essential to create a viable market and supply chain for compliant products and services. ## Funding & Sustainability Initial funding could be sought from federal and emirate-level budgets allocated for public health and environmental protection, potentially supplemented by green bonds or corporate social responsibility (CSR) partnerships. The incentive program's long-term sustainability could be supported by gradually shifting the subsidy burden to a market-based model, where certified installations lead to energy savings (via cleaner coils) and health cost reductions, creating a tangible return on investment for building owners. ## What Makes It New While existing programs like Al Sa'fat address building sustainability, this initiative specifically targets indoor air pollution through a mandated and incentivized focus on filtration performance. It directly addresses the identified pollutant of major concern—particulate matter—by creating a systematic, nationwide approach to improving the protective function of the indoor environments where people spend most of their time, complementing outdoor air quality efforts. ## Measuring Impact Key performance indicators would be proposed, including: the percentage of public school classrooms and government offices meeting the new IAQ standard; the number of households and private businesses participating in the incentive program; and pre- and post-installation measurements of indoor PM2.5 concentrations in a representative sample of participating buildings. Success could be measured against a proposed target of achieving WHO PM2.5 guideline levels indoors in a significant portion of certified spaces by 2040. ## Risks & Mitigation Key risks include increased energy consumption from higher-grade filters, which could be mitigated by promoting filters balanced for efficiency and mandating regular maintenance. Low public uptake in the private sector could be addressed through targeted awareness campaigns demonstrating health benefits and cost savings. Ensuring equitable access across income levels would require designing tiered incentives. Technical challenges in retrofitting older AC systems would necessitate developing clear guidelines and training programs for HVAC technicians.

text_key: ## One-Sentence Summary This initiative proposes the creation of a unified, real-time national air quality intelligence platform that integrates hyperlocal monitoring, predictive dust and ozone modeling, and personalized public alerts to empower informed behavior and reduce exposure to harmful pollution. ## Problem While monitoring infrastructure exists, public access to actionable, forecast-level air quality data is limited. Key pollutants like PM2.5 and ozone significantly exceed WHO guidelines, with dust a major driver. The public and vulnerable groups often lack timely, location-specific information to mitigate exposure during high-pollution events, such as dust storms in March-April or summer ozone peaks. This gap limits the protective utility of existing monitoring data. ## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases Primary beneficiaries include individuals with respiratory or cardiovascular conditions, outdoor workers, schools planning outdoor activities, and the general public seeking to protect their health. Use cases include: a parent checking a morning forecast for PM10 to decide if a child's sports day should proceed; a construction manager receiving an alert to mandate respirators for crews; and a person with asthma getting a personalized ozone warning to adjust their evening walk. ## Solution / Service Overview The proposed UAE-AQIP would be a central digital platform (app and web) providing: 1. **Real-time and Forecast Maps:** Integrating data from all federal and emirate-level monitoring stations with a unified, color-coded interface showing current and 48-hour forecasts for PM2.5, PM10, O3, and NO2. 2. **Dust & Ozone Prediction Engine:** A proposed modeling system, leveraging historical data on dust source directions and summer temperature correlations, to generate enhanced forecasts for these priority pollutants. 3. **Personalized Alerts:** Users can set location and pollutant thresholds (e.g., PM10 > 150 µg/m³) to receive push notifications with health advice. 4. **Open Data Portal:** A machine-readable API for researchers, developers, and businesses to build complementary services. ## Delivery Model The platform would be developed and maintained by a proposed dedicated unit within MOCCAE, in technical partnership with the National Center of Meteorology (for modeling) and each emirate's environmental agency (for data integration). A phased rollout could begin with a pilot in Abu Dhabi and Dubai, leveraging their existing station networks. ## Funding & Sustainability Initial development could be proposed for funding under the National Air Quality Agenda 2031. Operational sustainability could be explored through a mixed model: core government funding for public data and alerts, complemented by a proposed premium API tier for commercial users and potential sponsorship for non-health-related features (e.g., visibility forecasts for aviation/logistics). ## What Makes It New This initiative moves beyond static data display to provide predictive, personalized intelligence. It uniquely proposes to synthesize federal and emirate-level data into a single national forecast product, with a specific focus on modeling the UAE's dominant pollution drivers—dust and summer ozone—to provide genuinely actionable forecasts, not just retrospective measurements. ## Measuring Impact Success would be measured by proposed KPIs including: (1) platform adoption rate (e.g., registered users), (2) percentage of high-pollution days (AQI > 150) for which accurate forecasts were issued 24 hours in advance, (3) user survey reports of behavior change (e.g., reducing outdoor activity during alerts), and (4) increased utilization of the open data API by third parties. ## Risks & Mitigation Key risks include: **Data inconsistencies** between emirates—mitigated by establishing a proposed federal technical committee to standardize calibration and reporting. **Model inaccuracy**—mitigated by starting with a pilot region and continuously validating forecasts against monitoring data. **Public alert fatigue**—mitigated by allowing granular user customization of alerts and coupling them with clear, concise health guidance. **Funding uncertainty**—mitigated by securing initial project funding as a flagship digital component of the National Air Quality Agenda.

## Problem
While monitoring infrastructure exists, public access to actionable, forecast-level air quality data is limited. Key pollutants like PM2.5 and ozone significantly exceed WHO guidelines, with dust a major driver. The public and vulnerable groups often lack timely, location-specific information to mitigate exposure during high-pollution events, such as dust storms in March-April or summer ozone peaks. This gap limits the protective utility of existing monitoring data.

## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases
Primary beneficiaries include individuals with respiratory or cardiovascular conditions, outdoor workers, schools planning outdoor activities, and the general public seeking to protect their health. Use cases include: a parent checking a morning forecast for PM10 to decide if a child's sports day should proceed; a construction manager receiving an alert to mandate respirators for crews; and a person with asthma getting a personalized ozone warning to adjust their evening walk.

## Solution / Service Overview
The proposed UAE-AQIP would be a central digital platform (app and web) providing:
1. **Real-time and Forecast Maps:** Integrating data from all federal and emirate-level monitoring stations with a unified, color-coded interface showing current and 48-hour forecasts for PM2.5, PM10, O3, and NO2.
2. **Dust & Ozone Prediction Engine:** A proposed modeling system, leveraging historical data on dust source directions and summer temperature correlations, to generate enhanced forecasts for these priority pollutants.
3. **Personalized Alerts:** Users can set location and pollutant thresholds (e.g., PM10 > 150 µg/m³) to receive push notifications with health advice.
4. **Open Data Portal:** A machine-readable API for researchers, developers, and businesses to build complementary services.

## Delivery Model
The platform would be developed and maintained by a proposed dedicated unit within MOCCAE, in technical partnership with the National Center of Meteorology (for modeling) and each emirate's environmental agency (for data integration). A phased rollout could begin with a pilot in Abu Dhabi and Dubai, leveraging their existing station networks.

## Funding & Sustainability
Initial development could be proposed for funding under the National Air Quality Agenda 2031. Operational sustainability could be explored through a mixed model: core government funding for public data and alerts, complemented by a proposed premium API tier for commercial users and potential sponsorship for non-health-related features (e.g., visibility forecasts for aviation/logistics).

## What Makes It New
This initiative moves beyond static data display to provide predictive, personalized intelligence. It uniquely proposes to synthesize federal and emirate-level data into a single national forecast product, with a specific focus on modeling the UAE's dominant pollution drivers—dust and summer ozone—to provide genuinely actionable forecasts, not just retrospective measurements.

## Measuring Impact
Success would be measured by proposed KPIs including: (1) platform adoption rate (e.g., registered users), (2) percentage of high-pollution days (AQI > 150) for which accurate forecasts were issued 24 hours in advance, (3) user survey reports of behavior change (e.g., reducing outdoor activity during alerts), and (4) increased utilization of the open data API by third parties.

## Risks & Mitigation
Key risks include: **Data inconsistencies** between emirates—mitigated by establishing a proposed federal technical committee to standardize calibration and reporting. **Model inaccuracy**—mitigated by starting with a pilot region and continuously validating forecasts against monitoring data. **Public alert fatigue**—mitigated by allowing granular user customization of alerts and coupling them with clear, concise health guidance. **Funding uncertainty**—mitigated by securing initial project funding as a flagship digital component of the National Air Quality Agenda.

text_key: ## One-Sentence Summary DustSafe Protect is a proposed national air-quality shield that converts PM2.5, PM10 and ozone data into pre-agreed protective actions for children, older residents, people with asthma and outdoor workers. ## Problem UAE air pollution remains a health threat. EAD named particulate matter and ground-level ozone as Abu Dhabi's pollutants of major concern. IQAir gave UAE average PM2.5 as 36.4 µg/m³ in 2025, 7.3 times the WHO annual guideline of 5 µg/m³. An Abu Dhabi study found summer maximums of 218 µg/m³ for PM10 and 60 µg/m³ for PM2.5, with a PM2.5/PM10 ratio generally below 0.5, pointing to dust as the main driver. About 90% of UAE dust episodes come from the southwest, dust storms peak in winter, and most dust events fall in March and April. Summer ozone peaks in July and August and correlates strongly with temperature. Air pollution caused nearly 12% of UAE deaths in 2019, according to HEI/IHME. ## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases Children: pause outdoor PE and improve classroom filtration during dust events. Older people: receive multilingual alerts and access cooled, filtered community rooms on high-PM days. People with asthma: get personalized risk windows, inhaler check reminders, and clinic links during ozone peaks. Outdoor workers: receive work-stoppage triggers, filtered masks, shaded hydration points, and employer exposure logs. ## Solution / Service Overview Create a proposed Vulnerable Group Air Quality Protocol built on the national AQI method, which follows the US EPA method and covers 5 pollutants. It would combine: - Targeted alerts: SMS/WhatsApp notifications to schools, clinics, employers and caregivers when PM10, PM2.5 or ozone crosses protective thresholds. - Protection hubs: designated indoor rooms in schools, community centres, clinics and worker camps with filtered air, water, rest seating and asthma supplies. - Exposure management: a proposed digital log for outdoor employers to record work-stoppage hours, mask distribution and risk conditions. ## Delivery Model A proposed two-year pilot in Abu Dhabi and Dubai would use existing monitoring capacity: MOCCAE reclassified 64 monitoring stations nationally in 2023, EAD ran 20 fixed and 2 mobile monitoring stations in 2021, and Dubai Municipality operated more than 72 fixed monitoring stations in 2020. A dedicated programme unit would coordinate with schools, municipalities, employers and health facilities, without requiring new legislation. Phase 1: map high-risk sites. Phase 2: register beneficiaries and issue alert rules. Phase 3: test protection hubs and outdoor-work triggers during March-April dust episodes and July-August ozone peaks. ## Funding & Sustainability Funding would be proposed through an initial federal/Emirate allocation, employer contributions for outdoor-worker kits, and in-kind use of existing monitoring and community facilities. Sustainability would rely on measurable cost avoidance: Economist Impact estimated savings from meeting WHO guidelines at US$596 million a year. Employer incentives could reward companies meeting exposure-log targets. ## What Makes It New The initiative shifts from reporting air quality to protecting people. Instead of asking vulnerable groups to interpret AQI, it delivers pre-agreed actions: stop outdoor work, move children indoors, open filtered hubs, and trigger asthma care. It links dust and ozone seasonality to concrete schedules, making protection operational rather than advisory. ## Measuring Impact Proposed KPIs: percentage of registered sites receiving alerts within 15 minutes; hours of outdoor work avoided on high-risk days; uptake of protection hubs; reduction in reported asthma exacerbation visits during alert periods; and compliance with protective thresholds. Success would be judged by improved protection coverage, not only pollutant reductions. ## Risks & Mitigation Risks include alert fatigue, unequal access to hubs, privacy concerns over worker logs, and reliance on station data that may not capture local variation. Mitigation would use tiered alerts, multilingual communication, community-based hub siting, anonymized employer reporting, and proposed supplemental sensors at selected schools and worker camps.

text_key: ## One-Sentence Summary A proposed UAE-wide “Cool Green Corridors” programme would design shaded, low-emission urban routes and dust-buffer green zones to reduce heat, dust exposure and conditions that intensify summer ozone peaks. ## Problem UAE ambient PM2.5 was 33.7 µg/m³ in 2024 and 36.4 µg/m³ in 2025, far above the WHO annual guideline of 5 µg/m³. EAD named particulate matter and ground-level ozone as Abu Dhabi’s major pollutants of concern. Dust is key: an Abu Dhabi study found summer maximums of 218 µg/m³ PM10 and 60 µg/m³ PM2.5, with PM2.5/PM10 generally below 0.5. About 90% of UAE dust episodes come from the southwest, and most events fall in March and April. Summer ozone peaks in July and August and correlates strongly with temperature. Air pollution caused nearly 12% of UAE deaths in 2019, according to HEI/IHME. ## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases Beneficiaries would include residents walking, cycling or waiting for transport in high-exposure districts; school children; older adults; people with respiratory or cardiovascular conditions; outdoor workers; and neighbourhoods near roads, industry and dust pathways. Use cases would include shaded walking routes, school streets, bus stops, pedestrian links near metro stations, and green buffers between roads, industry and homes. ## Solution / Service Overview The programme would create “cool green corridors” in dense urban areas and “dust-buffer zones” on prevailing southwest exposure paths. Corridors would use shade canopies, reflective paving, low-VOC native planting and wind-flow design to reduce heat and dust entrainment. Green buffers would use species selected to avoid high volatile organic compound emissions, since ozone peaks correlate with temperature. The programme would also include micro-exposure mapping, community route guidance and design standards for new public spaces. ## Delivery Model A proposed delivery model would pair national air-quality planning with municipal implementation. It would be designed to complement MOCCAE’s National Air Quality Agenda 2031, which has an outdoor air area with 8 goals and 29 action themes. Municipalities, transport authorities, developers and schools could adopt corridor designs through planning conditions and public-space upgrades. A proposed coordination unit could set species lists, cooling design rules, monitoring protocols and maintenance requirements. Existing monitoring networks, such as MOCCAE’s reclassified stations, EAD stations and Dubai Municipality stations, could be used where available, with planned additional local sensors for pilot corridors. ## Funding & Sustainability Funding would be sought from municipal public-space budgets, green-building programmes, transport and health partnerships, and private sponsors. Dubai’s Al Sa’fat system has required Silver for new buildings since October 2020, so corridor elements could be integrated into future sustainable-building projects. Maintenance would be built into long-term landscape and road contracts, with water-efficient native planting and shade structures to reduce lifecycle costs. ## What Makes It New The initiative would connect dust exposure, heat and ozone formation, usually treated separately. Rather than only reducing emissions at source, it would reshape everyday urban routes to lower personal exposure and cool surfaces and air that intensify summer ozone peaks. It would use southwest dust-path knowledge, temperature-linked ozone data and urban design standards as one public-health service. ## Measuring Impact Proposed indicators would include PM10 and PM2.5 at corridor sites, surface and air temperature, ozone during July and August, dust-event exposure, pedestrian use and perceived comfort. Pilot corridors would be compared with similar untreated streets before and after installation. The programme would report against WHO annual guidelines and national AQI, while testing whether cooler, shaded, low-VOC corridors reduce exposure during dust episodes and summer ozone peaks. ## Risks & Mitigation Risks include water demand, poor species selection, maintenance gaps and uneven benefits. ## One-Sentence Summary
A proposed UAE-wide “Cool Green Corridors” programme would design shaded, low-emission urban routes and dust-buffer green zones to reduce heat, dust exposure and conditions that intensify summer ozone peaks.

## Problem
UAE ambient PM2.5 was 33.7 µg/m³ in 2024 and 36.4 µg/m³ in 2025, far above the WHO annual guideline of 5 µg/m³. EAD named particulate matter and ground-level ozone as Abu Dhabi’s major pollutants of concern. Dust is key: an Abu Dhabi study found summer maximums of 218 µg/m³ PM10 and 60 µg/m³ PM2.5, with PM2.5/PM10 generally below 0.5. About 90% of UAE dust episodes come from the southwest, and most events fall in March and April. Summer ozone peaks in July and August and correlates strongly with temperature. Air pollution caused nearly 12% of UAE deaths in 2019, according to HEI/IHME.

## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases
Beneficiaries would include residents walking, cycling or waiting for transport in high-exposure districts; school children; older adults; people with respiratory or cardiovascular conditions; outdoor workers; and neighbourhoods near roads, industry and dust pathways. Use cases would include shaded walking routes, school streets, bus stops, pedestrian links near metro stations, and green buffers between roads, industry and homes.

## Solution / Service Overview
The programme would create “cool green corridors” in dense urban areas and “dust-buffer zones” on prevailing southwest exposure paths. Corridors would use shade canopies, reflective paving, low-VOC native planting and wind-flow design to reduce heat and dust entrainment. Green buffers would use species selected to avoid high volatile organic compound emissions, since ozone peaks correlate with temperature. The programme would also include micro-exposure mapping, community route guidance and design standards for new public spaces.

## Delivery Model
A proposed delivery model would pair national air-quality planning with municipal implementation. It would be designed to complement MOCCAE’s National Air Quality Agenda 2031, which has an outdoor air area with 8 goals and 29 action themes. Municipalities, transport authorities, developers and schools could adopt corridor designs through planning conditions and public-space upgrades. A proposed coordination unit could set species lists, cooling design rules, monitoring protocols and maintenance requirements. Existing monitoring networks, such as MOCCAE’s reclassified stations, EAD stations and Dubai Municipality stations, could be used where available, with planned additional local sensors for pilot corridors.

## Funding & Sustainability
Funding would be sought from municipal public-space budgets, green-building programmes, transport and health partnerships, and private sponsors. Dubai’s Al Sa’fat system has required Silver for new buildings since October 2020, so corridor elements could be integrated into future sustainable-building projects. Maintenance would be built into long-term landscape and road contracts, with water-efficient native planting and shade structures to reduce lifecycle costs.

## What Makes It New
The initiative would connect dust exposure, heat and ozone formation, usually treated separately. Rather than only reducing emissions at source, it would reshape everyday urban routes to lower personal exposure and cool surfaces and air that intensify summer ozone peaks. It would use southwest dust-path knowledge, temperature-linked ozone data and urban design standards as one public-health service.

## Measuring Impact
Proposed indicators would include PM10 and PM2.5 at corridor sites, surface and air temperature, ozone during July and August, dust-event exposure, pedestrian use and perceived comfort. Pilot corridors would be compared with similar untreated streets before and after installation. The programme would report against WHO annual guidelines and national AQI, while testing whether cooler, shaded, low-VOC corridors reduce exposure during dust episodes and summer ozone peaks.

## Risks & Mitigation
Risks include water demand, poor species selection, maintenance gaps and uneven benefits. Mitigation would use native drought-tolerant plants, low-VOC species lists, clear maintenance contracts, phased pilots and community feedback. Design should avoid trapping pollutants in narrow streets and should preserve ventilation corridors.

Ongoing operations would be sustained through transaction fees on allowance auctions and credit registry transactions. text_key: --- BEGIN PROJECT --- ## One-Sentence Summary A proposed federal performance standard that mandates large industrial facilities in heavy-emitting sectors (cement, aluminium, steel, petrochemicals) to achieve a defined, progressively tightening annual reduction in their emissions intensity for key pollutants, with compliance demonstrated via continuous emissions monitoring systems and incentivized by a sliding scale of fees and rewards. ## Problem While dust is a major component of particulate matter in the UAE, human-made pollution from industrial sources remains a significant contributor to ambient air pollution and its associated health burdens. The context brief notes that oil and gas, road transport, and industry are among Abu Dhabi's biggest contributors. For heavy industry, there is a gap between existing ambient air quality standards and a direct, performance-based regulatory mechanism that drives continuous, verifiable reductions in emission intensity from these major point sources. This initiative targets the industrial segment of the pollution portfolio. A critical, related problem is the current fragmentation and opacity of industrial emissions data, which hinders evidence-based policy, public accountability, and investor confidence in the environmental performance of key economic sectors. ## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases The primary beneficiaries are the public health system and residents of the UAE, particularly in communities near industrial clusters. The regulated entities are major facilities in the cement, aluminium, steel, and petrochemical sectors. A proposed pilot could initially focus on a select group of such facilities in industrial zones like Jebel Ali, Mussafah, or Ruwais. ## Solution / Service Overview The proposed National Industrial Efficiency and Abatement Performance Standard (NIEAPS) would establish sector-specific, output-based benchmarks for emissions intensity (e.g., kg of pollutant per tonne of product) for PM10, PM2.5, NO2, and SO2. These benchmarks would be set below current average performance levels and would ratchet down on a defined five-year schedule. Each facility's compliance would be determined by data from mandated, certified Continuous Emissions Monitoring Systems (CEMS), with the data streamed to a proposed federal verification platform. ## Delivery Model The standard would be developed and enforced by the proposed federal air quality regulator, potentially operating under the auspices of the National Air Quality Agenda 2031. Implementation would involve: 1) Establishing a technical committee to set initial benchmarks; 2) Requiring regulated facilities to install and certify CEMS; 3) Launching a central data aggregation and verification platform; and 4) Administering a proposed financial mechanism where facilities exceeding their intensity target pay a fee, while those beating their target receive a proportional rebate on associated regulatory costs. ## Funding & Sustainability Initial funding for the regulatory platform and administration could be sought from federal budgets aligned with the National Air Quality Agenda. The proposed fee-and-rebate mechanism is designed to be revenue-neutral over time, with fees from under-performers funding rebates for top performers, thereby creating a continuous market incentive for improvement without a permanent drain on public funds. Facilities would bear the capital cost of CEMS installation. ## What Makes It New While the UAE has ambient air quality standards and green building codes, this initiative proposes a first-of-its-kind, sector-specific, intensity-based performance standard directly targeting heavy industry. It moves beyond setting ambient limits to regulating the production process itself. It innovates by linking verified CEMS data directly to a transparent, predictable financial incentive structure, creating a clear business case for pollution abatement investments. ## Measuring Impact Success would be measured by: 1) The percentage of regulated facilities in full compliance with their annual intensity targets; 2) The aggregate reduction in reported emissions of target pollutants from the regulated sector; 3) The trend in ambient air quality readings downwind of major industrial zones; and 4) Progress toward the National Air Quality Agenda's reported goal of 90% compliance with a national PM2.5 standard by 2040. The CEMS data would provide an unprecedented high-resolution dataset for tracking industrial emissions. ## Risks & Mitigation Key risks include: 1) **Industrial Competitiveness**: Stringent standards could be seen as a cost burden. Mitigation: The intensity-based design allows efficient producers to thrive, and the rebate system rewards leaders. A phased implementation would provide adjustment time. 2) **Data Integrity**: CEMS data could be manipulated. Mitigation: Strict certification protocols, third-party audits, and tamper-proof data logging would be required. 3) **Regulatory Capacity**: A new regulator may lack technical expertise. Mitigation: A proposed phased pilot would build capacity, and partnerships with academic institutions (e.g., Khalifa University) could provide technical support. --- END PROJECT ---

text_key: ## One-Sentence Summary This initiative proposes the development of a federal Indoor Air Quality (IAQ) Enhancement Framework, featuring a government-backed certification and incentive program for the widespread deployment of high-efficiency filtration in air-conditioning (AC) systems and standalone air cleaners within homes, schools, and offices. ## Problem While outdoor air quality initiatives exist, individuals spend the majority of their time indoors, where air pollution can also concentrate. Data indicates that PM2.5 and PM10 levels in the UAE significantly exceed WHO annual guidelines, with dust being a primary driver. Although AC systems are ubiquitous, their standard filters are typically ineffective at capturing fine particulate matter (PM2.5), leaving indoor environments vulnerable to infiltration of outdoor pollutants. This creates a critical health exposure gap, especially for vulnerable groups, undermining public health gains from outdoor emission reductions. ## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases Primary beneficiaries include residents in high-exposure areas, children in public and private schools, and employees in both government and private-sector offices. A proposed initial focus could be on vulnerable populations, including the elderly and those with respiratory conditions, as well as educational facilities where children's developing lungs are particularly susceptible. A proposed expansion of target beneficiaries includes the tourism and hospitality sector, where maintaining high indoor air quality could be framed as a component of service excellence and a competitive advantage for hotels, shopping malls, and long-stay serviced apartments. Use cases center on retrofitting existing AC systems with high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) or MERV-13+ filters and deploying standalone air purifiers in spaces where central system upgrades are impractical. ## Solution / Service Overview The proposed solution is a three-pillar framework: 1) A Federal IAQ Standard for Public Buildings, mandating minimum filtration efficiency (e.g., MERV-13) for new and retrofitted AC systems in schools, government offices, and healthcare facilities; 2) An IAQ Certification & Incentive Program for private residences and commercial buildings, offering subsidies, low-interest loans, or utility rebates for the installation of certified high-performance filtration systems; and 3) A Public Awareness Campaign on IAQ management, including guidance on filter maintenance and the benefits of air purification. ## Delivery Model The initiative would require collaboration between federal and emirate-level entities. A proposed governance structure could involve MOCCAE setting the federal standards and framework, while local municipalities (e.g., Dubai Municipality, Abu Dhabi's EAD) oversee implementation and enforcement within their jurisdictions. Partnerships with AC manufacturers, filter producers, and certified installers would be essential to create a viable market and supply chain for compliant products and services. ## Funding & Sustainability Initial funding could be sought from federal and emirate-level budgets allocated for public health and environmental protection, potentially supplemented by green bonds or corporate social responsibility (CSR) partnerships. The incentive program's long-term sustainability could be supported by gradually shifting the subsidy burden to a market-based model, where certified installations lead to energy savings (via cleaner coils) and health cost reductions, creating a tangible return on investment for building owners. ## What Makes It New While existing programs like Al Sa'fat address building sustainability, this initiative specifically targets indoor air pollution through a mandated and incentivized focus on filtration performance. It directly addresses the identified pollutant of major concern—particulate matter—by creating a systematic, nationwide approach to improving the protective function of the indoor environments where people spend most of their time, complementing outdoor air quality efforts. ## Measuring Impact Key performance indicators would be proposed, including: the percentage of public school classrooms and government offices meeting the new IAQ standard; the number of households and private businesses participating in the incentive program; and pre- and post-installation measurements of indoor PM2.5 concentrations in a representative sample of participating buildings. Success could be measured against a proposed target of achieving WHO PM2.5 guideline levels indoors in a significant portion of certified spaces by 2040. ## Risks & Mitigation Key risks include increased energy consumption from higher-grade filters, which could be mitigated by promoting filters balanced for efficiency and mandating regular maintenance. Low public uptake in the private sector could be addressed through targeted awareness campaigns demonstrating health benefits and cost savings. Ensuring equitable access across income levels would require designing tiered incentives. Technical challenges in retrofitting older AC systems would necessitate developing clear guidelines and training programs for HVAC technicians.

(3) Potential for increased operational costs for shipping lines, mitigated by clear long-term regulatory certainty and the proposed ECA potentially driving regional adoption, leveling the playing field. - Licensed ride-hailing and taxi companies operating in Abu Dhabi, Dubai, and other emirates.
- Last-mile delivery and logistics fleets serving urban areas.
These fleets are ideal first adopters due to their high fuel costs (making operational savings significant), centralized management, and fixed depot locations that facilitate charging infrastructure installation.

## Solution / Service Overview
The proposed initiative would have three core components: (1) A federal regulation mandating that all licensed high-mileage commercial fleets in urban areas transition a defined percentage of their vehicles to zero-emission models within a proposed target timeline. (2) A requirement for the simultaneous scrappage of existing, operational internal combustion engine vehicles from the operator's fleet to be eligible for support. (3) A federal grant and low-interest loan program to support the acquisition of new battery-electric vehicles and the installation of depot-based charging infrastructure.

## Delivery Model
A proposed federal entity, such as MOCCAE, would administer the grant application, loan program, and regulatory compliance through a dedicated digital portal. Partnering with relevant emirate-level transportation and economic authorities (e.g., Dubai's RTA, Abu Dhabi's DMT) would be essential for validating operator licenses and integrating the program with existing commercial vehicle regulations. Charging infrastructure support could be coordinated with existing utilities and standardization authorities to ensure technical and safety standards.

## Funding & Sustainability
Initial funding could be proposed from a combination of a reallocated portion of existing federal fuel subsidy expenditures and a proposed modest, per-kilometer levy on the operations of participating commercial fleets, creating a dedicated "Urban Fleet Transition Fund." This fund would finance vehicle purchase incentives, charging infrastructure grants, and low-interest loans. Long-term sustainability is designed to be finite; the direct financial incentives would be phased out over a proposed window, with the business case for operators built on the significantly lower per-kilometer energy and maintenance costs of EVs.

## What Makes It New
This initiative creates a unified, nationwide regulatory framework specifically targeting the highest-impact urban mobile pollution sources. It combines a mandatory fleet transition timeline with comprehensive financial and infrastructural support, addressing both vehicle replacement and enabling infrastructure in one integrated policy. Unlike broad consumer incentives, it leverages the rational economic calculus and centralized management of commercial fleet operators to achieve rapid, measurable turnover and tangible air quality improvements in the near term.

Key performance indicators would be proposed to track:
- Number of high-mileage internal combustion engine vehicles scrapped and replaced with zero-emission vehicles under the mandate.
- Aggregate reduction in estimated tailpipe emissions of NOx and PM, based on vehicle mileage data.
- Growth in depot-based fast-charging ports installed as part of the program.
- Post-implementation air quality monitoring data near high-traffic corridors, with analysis to isolate local vehicle contribution from regional dust.

*Risk 1:* Grid capacity strain from concentrated EV charging. *Mitigation:* Proposed program design encourages overnight depot charging and could include time-of-use rate incentives.
*Risk 2:* Regulatory compliance costs disproportionately burden smaller operators. *Mitigation:* A proposed tiered support structure or a quota for small and medium-sized enterprise operators could be explored within the financial program.
*Risk 3:* Inadequate vehicle model availability or suitability for UAE climate. *Mitigation:* Proposed eligibility would require vehicles to meet certified range and thermal management performance standards.
*Risk 4:* Increased upstream power generation emissions offsetting vehicle benefits. *Mitigation:* The UAE's increasing clean energy share is proposed to mitigate this risk over the vehicle lifetime.

# One-Sentence Summary
A proposed federal initiative to create a unified, national system combining advanced, data-driven forecasting of dust and port-related pollution with targeted land stabilisation, aimed at directly reducing emissions and exposure for high-risk communities and workers near industrial zones.

## Problem
Elevated levels of particulate matter (PM), particularly PM10 and PM2.5, are a persistent air quality challenge in the UAE, with studies indicating a PM2.5/PM10 ratio generally below 0.5, pointing to dust as a primary driver. While human-made sources are significant, natural mineral dust contributes substantially to PM2.5, and dust events most frequently originate from the southwest and peak in spring. This natural dust exacerbates pollution levels, contributing to health impacts and hindering progress toward national air quality targets and WHO guidelines.

## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases
The primary beneficiaries would be communities living and working near major ports and industrial areas, who would experience reduced exposure to combined dust and anthropogenic pollutants. The initiative would also target high-risk groups such as children, the elderly, and those with respiratory conditions in these areas. Key use cases include providing advanced, integrated pollution warnings to port-adjacent schools, healthcare facilities, and industrial worksites to modify outdoor activities and operations.

## Solution / Service Overview
The proposed initiative would establish an integrated system with three core components: 1) A high-resolution, AI-enhanced forecasting and early warning platform capable of predicting the intensity and trajectory of dust events and port-emission plumes 48-72 hours in advance. 2) A targeted land stabilisation program focusing on identified dust-source hotspots, especially in the southwestern region, using sustainable soil binders and windbreak fencing. 3) A strategic ‘greening for dust suppression’ program that deploys drought-resistant, native ground-cover vegetation in stabilised areas and along key transport corridors to anchor soil and reduce particulate load.

## Delivery Model
The initiative could be overseen by a proposed inter-agency task force led by the federal environmental ministry, in collaboration with port authorities, meteorological institutes, and environmental agencies. Regulatory development and phased implementation would be centralized at the federal level to ensure consistency. The forecasting platform would be developed in a proposed partnership with national and international meteorological research institutes. Land stabilisation and greening would be implemented through contracted specialists, with federal oversight. Warnings and air quality information would be disseminated via a dedicated public app and integrated into government alert systems.

## Funding & Sustainability
A proposed long-term sustainability model could explore a combination of federal budget allocation aligned with the National Air Quality Agenda and a proposed modest levy on cargo handled at major ports, creating a dedicated "Clean Air Fund." This fund would finance the forecasting platform, land stabilisation projects, and greening programs. Long-term sustainability would derive from reduced public health costs, alignment with the UAE's net-zero goals, and potential contributions from businesses benefiting from reduced operational disruptions.

## What Makes It New
This initiative proposes a novel integration of hyper-local, multi-source pollution forecasting with targeted, data-driven physical intervention on the ground. It moves beyond sector-specific monitoring and general warnings to actively treating identified natural dust source zones with an engineered, nature-based approach. The proposed use of advanced forecasting combined with soil stabilisation techniques and native-species greening tailored to the arid UAE environment represents a focused, integrated systems approach not yet deployed at a national scale for this combined purpose.

## Measuring Impact
Success would be measured by proposed key performance indicators: 1) Reduction in PM10 and PM2.5 concentrations during forecasted high-pollution events in target downwind communities near ports and industrial areas. 2) Increase in the accuracy and lead time of integrated pollution event warnings. 3) Hectares of dust-source hotspots stabilised and greened annually. 4) Tracking public and institutional adoption of the early warning system in target zones. 5) Monitoring trends in pollutant ratios to isolate the impact on dust-driven pollution.

Green buffers would use species selected to avoid high volatile organic compound emissions, since ozone peaks correlate with temperature. The programme would also include micro-exposure mapping, community route guidance and design standards for new public spaces.

## Delivery Model
A proposed delivery model would pair national air-quality planning with municipal implementation. It would be designed to complement MOCCAE’s National Air Quality Agenda 2031, which has an outdoor air area with 8 goals and 29 action themes. Municipalities, transport authorities, developers and schools could adopt corridor designs through planning conditions and public-space upgrades. A proposed coordination unit could set species lists, cooling design rules, monitoring protocols and maintenance requirements. Existing monitoring networks, such as MOCCAE’s reclassified stations, EAD stations and Dubai Municipality stations, could be used where available, with planned additional local sensors for pilot corridors.

## Funding & Sustainability
Funding would be sought from municipal public-space budgets, green-building programmes, transport and health partnerships, and private sponsors. A proposed mechanism to enhance sustainability would be the exploration of a dedicated municipal-level environmental improvement levy on high-emission commercial activities, with revenues hypothecated (ring-fenced) for the creation and maintenance of cool green corridors and dust-buffer zones in affected communities. Dubai’s Al Sa’fat system has required Silver for new buildings since October 2020, so corridor elements could be integrated into future sustainable-building projects. Maintenance would be built into long-term landscape and road contracts, with water-efficient native planting and shade structures to reduce lifecycle costs.

## What Makes It New
The initiative would connect dust exposure, heat and ozone formation, usually treated separately. Rather than only reducing emissions at source, it would reshape everyday urban routes to lower personal exposure and cool surfaces and air that intensify summer ozone peaks. It would use southwest dust-path knowledge, temperature-linked ozone data and urban design standards as one public-health service.

## Measuring Impact
Proposed indicators would include PM10 and PM2.5 at corridor sites, surface and air temperature, ozone during July and August, dust-event exposure, pedestrian use and perceived comfort. Pilot corridors would be compared with similar untreated streets before and after installation. The programme would report against WHO annual guidelines and national AQI, while testing whether cooler, shaded, low-VOC corridors reduce exposure during dust episodes and summer ozone peaks.

Risks include water demand, poor species selection, maintenance gaps and uneven benefits. Mitigation would use native drought-tolerant plants, low-VOC species lists, clear maintenance contracts, phased pilots and community feedback. Design should avoid trapping pollutants in narrow streets and should preserve ventilation corridors.

## Problem
UAE ambient PM2.5 levels remain far above the WHO annual guideline of 5 µg/m³. Particulate matter and ground-level ozone are major pollutants of concern, with dust episodes significantly contributing to PM levels. Summer ozone peaks correlate strongly with temperature. Air pollution is a leading cause of mortality, creating a pressing public health challenge for residents in dense urban environments.

## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases
Beneficiaries would include residents walking, cycling or waiting for transport in high-exposure districts; school children; older adults; people with respiratory or cardiovascular conditions; outdoor workers; and neighbourhoods near roads, industry and dust pathways. Use cases would include shaded walking routes, school streets, bus stops, pedestrian links near metro stations, and green buffers between pollution sources and homes.

## Solution / Service Overview
The proposed initiative would have three core components: (1) A federal regulation mandating that all licensed high-mileage commercial fleets in urban areas transition a defined percentage of their vehicles to zero-emission models within a proposed target timeline. (2) A requirement for the simultaneous scrappage of existing, operational internal combustion engine vehicles from the operator's fleet to be eligible for support. (3) A federal grant and low-interest loan program, funded by a dedicated emissions levy, to support the acquisition of new battery-electric vehicles and the installation of depot-based charging infrastructure.

## Delivery Model
A proposed federal entity would administer the grant application, loan program, and regulatory compliance through a dedicated digital portal. Partnering with relevant emirate-level transportation, environmental, and municipal planning authorities would be essential for validating operator licenses, integrating the program with existing regulations, and ensuring alignment with urban exposure reduction goals. Charging infrastructure support could be coordinated with existing utilities and standardization authorities to ensure technical and safety standards.

## Funding & Sustainability
Initial funding could be generated through a proposed modest levy on cargo handled at major ports and on emissions from designated industrial facilities, creating a dedicated "Urban Air Quality Fund." This fund would finance the vehicle purchase incentives, charging infrastructure grants, and low-interest loans for the commercial fleet transition. Long-term sustainability would derive from the dedicated revenue stream, reduced public health costs, and the significantly lower per-kilometer operational costs for fleet operators post-transition.

This initiative creates a unified, nationwide regulatory framework that innovatively connects major emission sources with hyper-local exposure reduction. It combines a mandatory fleet transition timeline for the highest-impact urban mobile sources with comprehensive financial support derived directly from industrial and maritime polluters. This creates a direct funding link between polluters and the communities most affected, leveraging the rational economic calculus of fleet operators to achieve rapid, measurable turnover and tangible air quality improvements for vulnerable populations in the near term. **A proposed novel feature is the integration of a dynamic, performance-based allocation mechanism within the fund. # One-Sentence Summary

## Problem
While the UAE has set a National EV Policy target of 50% EV penetration by 2050, current air quality challenges require more immediate action in key urban sectors. Road transport is a major contributor to emissions in urban centers like Abu Dhabi. Particulate matter (PM) and ground-level ozone remain pollutants of major concern, with summer ozone peaks strongly correlating with temperature. Although a significant portion of PM2.5 originates from natural dust and long-range transport, locally controlled mobile sources are a critical intervention point. Accelerating the replacement of high-utilization internal combustion engine vehicles, particularly those that operate almost continuously in population-dense areas, can deliver disproportionate air quality benefits per vehicle converted.

## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases
Beneficiaries would include residents walking, cycling or waiting for transport in high-exposure districts; school children; older adults; people with respiratory or cardiovascular conditions; outdoor workers; and neighbourhoods near roads, industry and dust pathways. Use cases would include shaded walking routes, school streets, bus stops, pedestrian links near metro stations, and green buffers between pollution sources and homes.

## Solution / Service Overview
The proposed initiative would have three core components: (1) A federal regulation mandating that all licensed high-mileage commercial fleets in urban areas transition a defined percentage of their vehicles to zero-emission models within a proposed target timeline. (2) A requirement for the simultaneous scrappage of existing, operational internal combustion engine vehicles from the operator's fleet to be eligible for support. (3) A federal grant and low-interest loan program to support the acquisition of new battery-electric vehicles and the installation of depot-based charging infrastructure. (4) To maximize the initiative's impact and resource efficiency, a proposed vehicle-as-a-service (VaaS) procurement option would be integrated into the program. This would allow fleet operators, particularly small and medium-sized ones, to access zero-emission vehicles through qualified, local third-party service providers offering bundled vehicles, charging, and maintenance on a per-kilometer or monthly subscription basis, without requiring a large upfront capital outlay.

## Delivery Model
A proposed federal entity, such as MOCCAE, would administer the grant application, loan program, and regulatory compliance through a dedicated digital portal. Partnering with relevant emirate-level transportation and economic authorities (e.g., Dubai's RTA, Abu Dhabi's DMT) would be essential for validating operator licenses and integrating the program with existing commercial vehicle regulations. Charging infrastructure support could be coordinated with existing utilities and standardization authorities to ensure technical and safety standards.

## Funding & Sustainability
Initial funding could be generated through a proposed modest levy on cargo handled at major ports and on emissions from designated industrial facilities, creating a dedicated "Urban Air Quality Fund." This fund would finance the vehicle purchase incentives, charging infrastructure grants, and low-interest loans for the commercial fleet transition. Long-term sustainability would derive from the dedicated revenue stream, reduced public health costs, and the significantly lower per-kilometer operational costs for fleet operators post-transition.

This initiative creates a unified, nationwide regulatory framework that innovatively connects major emission sources with hyper-local exposure reduction. It combines a mandatory fleet transition timeline for the highest-impact urban mobile sources with comprehensive financial support derived directly from industrial and maritime polluters. # One-Sentence Summary
This initiative proposes a federal program to deploy targeted land stabilisation and strategic greening specifically around the high-utilization urban routes of commercial fleets, funded by a levy on industrial and maritime emissions, creating a direct, nature-based intervention to reduce fleet and public exposure to particulate matter.

## Problem
While the UAE has set a National EV Policy target, current air quality challenges require more immediate action in key urban sectors. Road transport is a major contributor to emissions in urban centers. Particulate matter (PM) and ground-level ozone remain pollutants of major concern, with summer ozone peaks strongly correlating with temperature. Although a significant portion of PM2.5 originates from natural dust, locally controlled mobile sources are a critical intervention point. Accelerating the replacement of high-utilization internal combustion engine vehicles, particularly those that operate almost continuously in population-dense areas, can deliver disproportionate air quality benefits per vehicle converted.

## Target Beneficiaries & Use Cases
The primary target beneficiaries are commercial fleet operators with high daily mileage and predictable urban routes. This includes licensed ride-hailing and taxi companies operating in major urban emirates, and last-mile delivery and logistics fleets serving urban areas. These fleets are ideal first adopters due to their high fuel costs, centralized management, and fixed depot locations that facilitate charging infrastructure installation.

## Solution / Service Overview
The proposed initiative would establish an integrated system with three core components: 1) A high-resolution, AI-enhanced dust forecasting and early warning platform capable of predicting the intensity and trajectory of dust events 48-72 hours in advance. 2) A targeted land stabilisation program focusing on identified dust-source hotspots, especially in the southwestern region, using sustainable soil binders and windbreak fencing. 3) A strategic ‘greening for dust suppression’ program that deploys drought-resistant, native ground-cover vegetation in stabilised areas and along key transport corridors to anchor soil.

## Delivery Model
Delivery would be coordinated by a proposed cross-emirate task force under federal leadership, leveraging existing monitoring networks. The forecasting platform would be developed in a proposed partnership with national and international meteorological research institutes. Land stabilisation and greening would be implemented through contracted specialists, with oversight from environmental agencies. Warnings and air quality information would be disseminated via a dedicated public app and integrated into existing government alert systems.

## Funding & Sustainability
Funding could be generated through a proposed modest levy on cargo handled at major ports and on emissions from designated industrial facilities, creating a dedicated "Urban Air Quality Fund." This fund would finance the vehicle purchase incentives, charging infrastructure grants, and low-interest loans for the commercial fleet transition to meet the performance standard. Long-term sustainability would derive from this dedicated revenue stream, reduced public health costs, and the lower per-kilometer operational costs for compliant fleet operators.

## What Makes It New
While dust forecasting exists, this initiative proposes a novel integration of hyper-local forecasting with targeted, data-driven physical intervention on the ground. It moves beyond monitoring and general warnings to actively treating identified source zones. The proposed use of advanced soil stabilisation techniques combined with native-species greening tailored to the arid UAE environment represents a focused, nature-based engineering approach not yet deployed at a national scale for this purpose.
